The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a proposed study by Harvard University aimed at understanding the behavior of aerosol particles in the stratosphere. Led by principal investigator Frank Keutsch, the initiative sought to enhance computer models assessing the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering, specifically solar radiation management. It is important to clarify that SCoPEx was not designed to deploy geoengineering or to cool the planet. The experiment planned to utilize a scientific balloon gondola operating at altitudes of approximately 20 km, releasing a very small quantity of calcium carbonate (100 grams to 2 kilograms) into a defined mixed volume to analyze aerosol microphysics and chemistry.

However, a planned platform test in Sweden in 2021 was limited to hardware testing, as the SCoPEx Advisory Committee advised postponement pending societal engagement, with no particles released. In March 2024, it was announced that Keutsch would no longer pursue SCoPEx, and the platform is now expected to be repurposed for unrelated stratospheric research. Concerns regarding ozone depletion and the chemical implications of different aerosol types remain significant issues in the discourse on solar geoengineering research.
